Q: What is the Best external dll for AES-GCM encrypt/decrypt for C# .Net 4.8.1 A:

Using anything other than a 12-byte nonce for AES/GCM is pretty much a waste of time. You certainly don't add any entropy to the encryption operation by using nonces larger than 12 bytes as nonces that aren't 12 bytes get "coerced" to 12 bytes anyway. So you gain nothing but the cost of the CPU cycles to change your "better" nonce to 12 bytes, unless you know exactly what you're doing and why. And even then you're likely to be wrong.

Q: How to get the keymap of the currently used keyboard? A:

Here is documentation for the xkbcommon-x11 API.

xkbcommon-x11

You can download it via package manager xkbcommon-x11.

It only has a few functions so it shouldn't be too hard to figure out. I believe this gets a keymap for a device.

The XKB extension supports using separate keymaps and states for different keyboard devices. The devices are identified by an integer device ID and are managed by another X11 extension, XInput. The original X11 protocol only had one keyboard device, called the core keyboard, which is still supported as a virtual device

You may want to use XInput to find a keyboard device. You could instead use the core keyboard device.

Q: Astrojs static vs SSR when dealing with pages calling endpoints A:

Astro JS is primarily a Static Site Generator.

And the final assembled site will be static.

If some dynamics are required, you can embed the necessary components as SPA components (possibly using React), and then implement the dynamics there.

This way, you'll get a static site with a touch of dynamics that fits well with SEO paradigms and other crawlers that value your resource's content.

Q: How do you apply WPF Fluent theme (+ Application.ThemeMode theme-aware) to a control's Background? A:

I decided to look into the source code of the actual fluent theme resource dictionaries in the dotnet/wpf repo, and I figured out that the brushes for background/foreground in WPF with fluent style are as follows.

  • ApplicationBackgroundBrush for background
  • TextFillColorPrimaryBrush for foreground

So to solve my specific problem, I can add this to the Border:

<Border Background="{DynamicResource ApplicationBackgroundBrush}">
</Border>

And yes, they do also animate during theme switches.

Q: Why are trait objects usually used via references (&dyn Trait) or smart Pointers (like Box<dyn Trait>)? A:

A better answer than "it doesn't compile" is why doesn't it compile.

In Rust, every variable starts out on the stack. Objects on the stack have a fixed size. However, think of the implementation of Trait. Any data in the universe can be used to implement this trait, so it can be anywhere from 1 byte, 64 bytes, or even zero bytes. So if you try to pass a dyn Trait, the compiler doesn't know its size.

The variable size means that it can't stay on the stack.

But why can't we allocate a dynamic-length object on the stack?

It's actually possible to do this. C++ has a rarely used feature called VLAs (variable-length arrays). However, as the history of C++ shows, just because something is possible, doesn't mean it's good practice.

Languages like C, C++, Rust, etc. and their ecosystems have generally decided against variable-length stack-allocated types, because they're unperformant, crash and vulnerability prone, and don't net much benefit over regular heap allocation.

To see why, consider what happens if Trait were a dynamically-sized stack type:

fn consume(obj: dyn Trait) {
  // Handle object here
}

This function could do anything with the type, move it around, drop it, pass it to other functions, etc.

If the implementor is in fact very big, this could lead to a lot of move operations. Also, it forces stack offsets to be calculated dynamically, which affects the performance of the entire function (as well as deeper functions called by it). Structs that store dynamically-sized types also become dynamically-sized.

Pretty soon you have an entire call graph with dynamic stack offsets and dynamic field offsets. Not a big deal, maybe? Sure, but it also makes your program a whole lot easier to crash. Imagine a dynamically-sized array that has more elements depending on user input. If the size is too big, you run out of stack space (which is much smaller than heap space), and the program goes down.

All these complications are why basically no one uses dynamically-sized stack allocation. It's way easier to compute static offsets to fields, or stack pointers, when sizes are known. And less hard to crash your program, too.

Q: elementor off-canvas is not visible on webview A:

try debugging the WebView with the followng

WebView.setWebContentsDebuggingEnabled(true);

Then open:

chrome://inspect

Check if:

  • The menu exists in DOM
  • It’s rendered but off-screen
  • It’s hidden via CSS stacking

Q: "export 'createStore' was not found in 'redux' A:

In the store.js replace

export const store = createStore(
  reducers,
  applyMiddleware(sagaMiddleware)
)

with

export const store = createStore(
  reducers,
  {},
  applyMiddleware(sagaMiddleware)
)
